Function catalogue

Source: vignettes/articles/function-catalogue.Rmd
function-catalogue.Rmd

Dynet exports 38 functions in six categories, plus 50 S3 methods across the result classes. Every verb addresses vertices by name and returns a tidy one-row-per-observation data frame.

Category Verbs What it does
Construction 4 Build a network from a relational log; read it back as a time series
Editing 17 Rewrite spells and vertex activity without breaking time
Measurement 8 Centrality, reachability, structure, mixing, turn-taking, burstiness, duration, similarity
Paths 5 Time-respecting paths and four views of the result
Structure 3 Turn the network into another object
Animation 1 Render the measurement grid as a film

Construction

dynet() builds a temporal network from a relational log. It takes a data frame of ties and a set of column selectors, infers one of four log formats from which selectors are named, and returns an object of class c("dynet", "netobject", "cograph_network") carrying the spell table, the node table and the construction metadata. The four formats are interval logs with explicit start and end times, contact logs of instantaneous events, threaded logs where an edge stays active until its thread falls silent, and co-presence logs where actors sharing a group become connected.

dn <- dynet(school_contacts)
dn
#> # Temporal network (interval format, directed) | a cograph netobject
#> # 14 vertices | 240 edge spells | 110 distinct pairs
#> # observed from 0 to 21.52 step, binned every 1
#> 
#>   from   to start  end duration weight
#>  Jonas  Dan  0.00 1.10     1.10      1
#>   Gita  Ana  0.14 0.98     0.84      1
#>    Leo Mira  0.15 0.42     0.27      1
#>    Leo Iris  0.15 0.96     0.81      1
#>   Kira  Ben  0.33 0.69     0.36      1
#>    Leo Iris  0.38 0.50     0.12      1
#> # 234 more spells. summary() describes the network; plot() draws it.

as_dynet() converts an object of another class to a temporal network. It takes that object and returns a dynet. The method for networkDynamic imports edge spells, vertex spells, the observation period and per-edge attributes. The method for dynet is the identity and returns its input unchanged, so the call is safe on an object that is already a temporal network.

events() counts edge formation and dissolution over time. It takes a network, a measure name, and the four grid arguments, and returns a dynet_metric at graph level with one row per time point and measure. Eight measures are available, from raw "formation" and "dissolution" counts through to the formation and dissolution rates, which divide confirmed transitions by exact eligible pair-time.

snapshots() slices the network into one edge list per time bin. It takes a network and the grid arguments and returns a dynet_snapshot data frame with one row per active edge per bin, holding time, from, to, weight and n_spells, preceded by session when the network has sessions. A pair joined by more than one spell inside one bin is a single edge, and n_spells records how many spells produced it.

bins <- snapshots(dn, step = 4)
bins
#> # Snapshot edges | 6 bins | 216 tie rows | time in step
#>    time  from    to weight n_spells
#> 1     0   Ana Jonas      2        2
#> 2     0 Jonas  Kira      1        1
#> 3     0 Jonas  Mira      1        1
#> 4     0 Jonas   Dan      1        1
#> 5     0  Kira   Leo      1        1
#> 6     0  Kira   Ben      1        1
#> 7     0  Kira   Eve      1        1
#> 8     0   Leo  Mira      1        1
#> 9     0   Leo  Finn      1        1
#> 10    0   Leo  Iris      2        2
#> # 206 more rows. summary() counts them by bin.

Editing

Seventeen verbs rewrite the spell table, the node table or the vertex-activity table. Each takes a network, returns a new one of class c("dynet", "netobject", "cograph_network"), and leaves its input unchanged. Edits go through a rebuild, so canonical spell identifiers can renumber after any of them.

Adding

add_nodes() adds vertices. It takes a character vector of names or a data frame with a name column and static attributes, and returns a network in which the new vertices are implicit always-active isolates until ties or vertex activity are supplied.

add_ties() adds tie spells. It takes a data frame of endpoints and times, and returns a network with the canonical temporal ties and every flattened cograph field rebuilt together. Columns beyond the canonical spell fields are carried as tie attributes.

add_arcs() is the directed counterpart of add_ties() and delegates to it.

add_vertex_spells() declares periods in which a vertex is present. It takes a data frame with node, start and end, and returns a network whose existing activity and the supplied spells are canonicalised together, so an added spell that overlaps or abuts an existing one for the same vertex is merged into it.

Removing

remove_nodes() removes vertices. It takes their names and a cascade flag, and returns a network without them and, under cascade = TRUE, without their ties and activity spells. At least one temporal tie must remain.

remove_ties() removes tie spells. It takes row positions, a condition over the spell table, or endpoint and time selectors, and returns a network without the matched spells. A request that matches nothing raises dynet_tie_not_found.

remove_arcs() is the directed counterpart of remove_ties().

remove_vertex_spells() drops declared activity components. It takes integer positions or a logical mask and returns a network with the rest canonicalised again, so the remaining spell identifiers renumber. A vertex left with no declaration becomes implicitly always active.

Updating and renaming

update_nodes() adds or replaces static vertex attributes. It takes a data frame with a name key and one or more attribute columns, and returns a network with the same spells, activity and metadata, and the attributes written onto the named vertices. Unnamed vertices keep their existing values.

update_ties() edits selected spells. It takes a selection and a data frame of replacement values, and returns a network holding the unselected spells unchanged and the selected ones with the supplied values substituted.

update_vertex_spells() edits selected activity components. It takes positions and a data frame of replacement fields, and returns a network in which the updated components are canonicalised with the retained ones. A column outside the vertex-spell schema raises dynet_unknown_column.

rename_nodes() renames vertices. It takes a named character vector, or an old/new data frame, and returns a network with edge endpoints, node attributes, vertex activity, cograph labels and groups renamed together.

rename_sessions() renames session labels. It takes the same mapping forms and returns a network with edge and vertex session labels renamed together and the session scheme in the metadata updated. Labels absent from the mapping are left alone.

Declaring support

set_observations() replaces the observation window. It takes either a two-column data frame of components or a start and end pair, and returns a network whose raw spells are unchanged and whose measurement view alone is replaced, so as.data.frame(x) still returns the originals.

clear_observations() restores implicit support. It takes a network and returns one observed continuously from its earliest raw start through its latest raw end, with every explicit observation field dropped from the metadata.

set_tie_sessions() assigns or removes session walls. It takes a character vector of length one or of the raw tie count, and returns a network with a session column on the spell table and the scheme recorded in metadata, or with both removed under session = NULL. A full-length vector is matched positionally against the sorted spell table, so labels should be derived from as.data.frame(dn).

set_vertex_spells() replaces declared vertex activity outright. It takes a vertex-spell data frame, or the string "ties" to declare each vertex present from its first tie to its last, and returns a network whose declared activity is exactly that.

present <- set_vertex_spells(dn, "ties")
present
#> # Temporal network (interval format, directed) | a cograph netobject
#> # 14 vertices | 240 edge spells | 110 distinct pairs
#> # observed from 0 to 21.52 step, binned every 1
#> 
#>   from   to start  end duration weight
#>  Jonas  Dan  0.00 1.10     1.10      1
#>   Gita  Ana  0.14 0.98     0.84      1
#>    Leo Mira  0.15 0.42     0.27      1
#>    Leo Iris  0.15 0.96     0.81      1
#>   Kira  Ben  0.33 0.69     0.36      1
#>    Leo Iris  0.38 0.50     0.12      1
#> # 234 more spells. summary() describes the network; plot() draws it.

Measurement

Eight verbs measure a network over time. Each returns a dynet_metric: a tidy data frame whose columns are ordered session, time, the unit of observation, measure and value. The session column appears only under sessions = "separate", which is the one mode that keeps session labels apart.

The grid arguments are not shared by all eight. dyn_centrality(), metrics(), mixing() and similarity() take all four; dyn_reachability() and pshifts() take start and end only; and burstiness() and durations() summarise the whole observed period.

dyn_centrality() computes vertex centrality. It takes one or more measure names and a scope, and returns one row per vertex, time point and measure. Nineteen measures are available at scope = "snapshot", which treats each time bin as a static graph, and four at scope = "temporal", which measures along time-respecting paths and reports no time column because the whole window yields one value per vertex.

between <- dyn_centrality(dn, measure = "betweenness")
between
#> # Betweenness (node-level)
#> # 14 vertices | 22 time points, 1 per bin | time in step
#>  time  node     measure value
#>     0   Ana betweenness     0
#>     0   Ben betweenness     0
#>     0  Cara betweenness     0
#>     0   Dan betweenness     0
#>     0   Eve betweenness     0
#>     0  Finn betweenness     0
#>     0  Gita betweenness     0
#>     0  Hugo betweenness     0
#>     0  Iris betweenness     1
#>     0 Jonas betweenness     0
#>     0  Kira betweenness     1
#>     0   Leo betweenness     0
#> # 296 more rows. summary() aggregates them; plot() draws them.

dyn_reachability() computes how much of the network each vertex can reach. It takes a direction and a measure name and returns one row per vertex per measure at node level. Proportions are labelled forward_reach and backward_reach, counts forward_reach_count and backward_reach_count. A vertex is excluded from its own reachable set.

metrics() computes graph-level structure. It takes one or more of forty measure names and returns one row per time point and measure. The measure "triads" contributes sixteen rows per time point, one per triad class.

density <- metrics(dn, measure = "density")
density
#> # Density (graph-level)
#> # 22 time points, 1 per bin | time in step
#>  time measure      value
#>     0 density 0.05494505
#>     1 density 0.04395604
#>     2 density 0.05494505
#>     3 density 0.06593407
#>     4 density 0.07142857
#>     5 density 0.08791209
#>     6 density 0.15934066
#>     7 density 0.10439560
#>     8 density 0.09890110
#>     9 density 0.08791209
#>    10 density 0.10439560
#>    11 density 0.09890110
#> # 10 more rows. summary() aggregates them; plot() draws them.

mixing() computes how much tie activity runs within and between vertex groups. It takes the name of a node attribute and returns one row per time point and ordered group pair, with from_group and to_group naming the pair.

pshifts() classifies consecutive turns into Gibson’s thirteen participation-shift types. It takes a directed network and an output shape, and returns a dynet_pshifts data frame. Under output = "final" that is thirteen rows, one per shift class, always all thirteen even when a class never occurred. Under "cumulative" it is thirteen rows per classified turn, carrying the running count.

burstiness() measures how unevenly each vertex’s events are spaced. It takes a measure name and returns one row per vertex and measure, with no time column. The burstiness coefficient is 1 in the bursty limit, 0 at the Poisson reference and -1 for perfectly regular activity; memory is the lag-1 correlation between consecutive inter-event gaps.

durations() measures how long relationships lasted. It takes a unit that selects the row identity and a measure name, and returns an edge-level table under unit = "pair" or "spell", and a node-level table under the vertex-activity units. The censored argument decides whether spells whose boundaries were never observed are retained.

similarity() compares the network at each pair of time points. It takes a coefficient name and returns a dynet_similarity data frame with one row per ordered pair of time bins and columns time, other, measure and value. The diagonal is included and is one for every coefficient except "hamming", where identical layers differ in nothing and score zero.

The shared grid

Four arguments decide when the network is measured, following tsna::tSnaStats():

Argument Meaning tsna equivalent
start, end First and last measurement start, end
step How often to measure time.interval
window How much time each measurement covers aggregate.dur

window == step tiles, window > step slides, window == 0 samples an instant, and window = "all" treats the whole observed period as one bin.

Paths

paths() finds time-respecting journeys from one vertex. It takes a network, a source vertex name, and a direction, and returns a dynet_paths data frame with one row per vertex: node, reachable, arrival_time, attained, latency, n_hops and n_paths. A journey is time-respecting when each hop leaves no earlier than the previous hop arrived. The criterion is foremost-then-shortest: earliest arrival first, fewest contacts second.

routes <- paths(dn, from = "Ana")
routes
#> # Time-respecting paths from 'Ana', from t = 0
#> # reaches 13 of 13 other vertices | time in step
#>   node reachable arrival_time attained latency n_hops n_paths
#>    Ana      TRUE         0.00     TRUE    0.00      0       1
#>    Ben      TRUE         9.59     TRUE    9.59      3       3
#>   Cara      TRUE         6.67     TRUE    6.67      1       1
#>    Dan      TRUE         7.98     TRUE    7.98      4       1
#>    Eve      TRUE        11.66     TRUE   11.66      4       3
#>   Finn      TRUE         6.96     TRUE    6.96      2       1
#>   Gita      TRUE         6.36     TRUE    6.36      2       1
#>   Hugo      TRUE         7.98     TRUE    7.98      3       1
#>   Iris      TRUE        10.00     TRUE   10.00      3       1
#>  Jonas      TRUE         2.12     TRUE    2.12      1       1
#>   Kira      TRUE         6.12     TRUE    6.12      2       2
#>    Leo      TRUE         9.65     TRUE    9.65      3       1
#> # 2 more rows. summary() aggregates them; plot() draws the tree.

pathways() counts the routes those journeys take. It takes a network, optionally one source, and returns a dynet_pathways data frame with one row per distinct route, most frequent first: route as the vertex sequence joined by arrows, endpoint, count, and share as the route’s fraction of all counted routes.

path_network() builds the union of the optimal routes. It takes a paths() result and returns a static dynet_path_network, whose edge table has one row per hop used by at least one optimal route and whose node table has one row per reached vertex. Unreachable vertices are absent rather than present with missing values.

path_trajectories() arranges the routes as a counted prefix tree. It takes a paths() result and a min_count threshold and returns a dynet_path_trajectories data frame with one row per tree node: node as the route prefix, parent, depth, count, probability, vertex, time, session and branch.

plot_path_trajectories() draws that tree. It takes a paths() or path_trajectories() result and a measure that decides what the fill encodes, and returns a ggplot object. Each vertex name is printed beside its value, so no distinction rests on colour alone.

A vertex with declared spells begins its search at its own first presence inside the window rather than at the window edge. A vertex never present in the window reaches nothing.

Structure and animation

projection() expands the network into vertex-time states. It takes the grid arguments and an interlayer coupling weight omega, and returns a dynet_projection holding two tables, reached with as.data.frame(x, what = "vertices") for the states and as.data.frame(x, what = "edges") for the directed arcs between them. Coupling is ordinal: each slice is joined to the next one only.

collapse_network() reduces temporal activity to one static weighted network. It takes a weight rule that decides what an edge weight means, from "binary" through to summed durations and spell counts, and returns a dynet_collapsed cograph netobject with an edge table and a node table. Under sessions = "separate" it returns one such object per session.

static <- collapse_network(dn)
static
#> # Collapsed temporal network | 14 vertices | 110 edges | weight: binary
#> # 0 to 21.52 step
#>  from    to binary union_duration total_duration duration_fraction spell_count
#>   Ana  Cara      1           0.10           0.10       0.004646840           1
#>   Ana   Dan      1           1.02           1.02       0.047397770           3
#>   Ana  Gita      1           1.99           2.11       0.092472119           5
#>   Ana  Iris      1           0.50           0.50       0.023234201           1
#>   Ana Jonas      1           2.34           2.34       0.108736059           4
#>   Ana  Kira      1           0.11           0.11       0.005111524           1
#>  weight_sum weighted_duration latest_weight first  last activity.duration
#>           1              0.10             1  6.67  6.77              0.10
#>           3              1.02             1 12.04 20.10              1.02
#>           5              2.11             1  6.57 14.16              1.99
#>           1              0.50             1 13.80 14.30              0.50
#>           4              2.34             1  2.12  9.13              2.34
#>           1              0.11             1 11.60 11.71              0.11
#>  activity.count
#>               1
#>               3
#>               5
#>               1
#>               4
#>               1

induce_subgraph() extracts a subgraph. It takes a condition over the node table, a condition over the spell table, or both, and returns a network carrying only the selected spells, the vertices they touch, those vertices’ activity spells, and all static attributes. Centralities are available as columns inside the nodes condition.

animate() renders the measurement grid as a film. It takes the same four grid arguments as every measuring verb, a file whose extension selects the encoder, and returns a dynet_animation data frame with one row per bin holding bin, frame, time, window_start, window_end, nodes, idle, ties, forming and dissolving. The table is returned invisibly, since writing the file is the purpose of the call. GIF output requires gifski; mp4 and webm require av.

Result classes

Every result class carries print, summary, plot and as.data.frame – 50 S3 methods in total. A secondary table always comes out through an argument, never by reaching in with $.

Class Returned by
dynet dynet(), as_dynet(), and every editing verb
dynet_metric dyn_centrality(), dyn_reachability(), metrics(), mixing(), burstiness(), durations(), events()
dynet_paths paths()
dynet_pathways pathways()
dynet_path_network path_network()
dynet_path_trajectories path_trajectories()
dynet_snapshot snapshots()
dynet_similarity similarity()
dynet_pshifts pshifts()
dynet_projection projection()
dynet_collapsed collapse_network()
dynet_animation animate()

Secondary tables arrive as as.data.frame(x, what = "steps"), as.data.frame(x, what = "vertex_spells"), as.data.frame(x, session = "s1") and the like.

On a measuring verb, plot = TRUE follows hist(): drawing is a side effect and the tidy result still comes back, invisibly when it has drawn.
